# m06-l01 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

Path of a Projectile.

A projectile is an object shot through the air; its path through space is its trajectory.

Our big question for this lesson: what forces affect a basketball's trajectory? Think about a hopping frog, a tossed snowball, and an arrow shot from a bow. They all follow similar paths. Each one rises and then falls, always curving downward along a parabola.

An object shot through the air is called a projectile, and its path through space is called its trajectory. If you know a projectile's initial velocity, you can figure out its trajectory. Figure 1 shows water launched horizontally and at an angle. Either way, gravity bends the path downward into a parabola.

You can draw a free-body diagram for a launched projectile, too. If you ignore air resistance, then once the initial force launches it, the only force acting on it through the air is gravity. And gravity is what curves it downward.

## Slide 3

Independence of Motion.

Projectile motion is a combination of constant-velocity horizontal motion and accelerated vertical motion.

Picture two softball players warming up, tossing high fly balls back and forth. The ball is a projectile, so it follows a parabolic path. But what you see depends on where you stand.

Stand directly behind one player, and the ball just seems to go up and come back down, like anything tossed straight up. Now float above the field in a hot-air balloon. From up there, the ball seems to slide from one player to the other at a constant speed, like a hockey puck gliding across ice. And from the sideline, you see the whole parabola. Projectile motion is a combination of these two motions. The same is true for a basketball shot: from behind the shooter it rises and falls, from above it moves in a straight line toward the hoop, and from the sideline it arcs.

Why do projectiles act this way? Once the softball leaves a player's hand, and if we ignore air resistance, no contact forces act on it. Only the field force of gravity pulls it down. So gravity gives the ball a downward acceleration, and nothing changes its sideways motion.

## Slide 4

Comparing Motion Diagrams.

A projectile's horizontal motion does not affect its vertical motion.

Figure 2 shows two balls. The red ball was dropped, and the blue ball was given an initial horizontal velocity of 2.0 meters per second. What's the same about their paths?

Look at their heights. The horizontal lines mark equal vertical distances. At every moment a picture was taken, the two balls were at the same height. Their vertical position changed by the same amount, so their average vertical velocities during each interval were the same too. And the growing vertical distance from one interval to the next shows that both were accelerating downward because of gravity. After falling for 1 second, each ball would be moving downward at 9.8 meters per second.

So the launched ball's horizontal motion doesn't affect its vertical motion. A horizontally launched projectile has an initial horizontal velocity but no initial vertical velocity. That's why its vertical motion matches an object dropped from rest. Like the red ball, the blue ball's downward velocity increases steadily because of the acceleration due to gravity.

## Slide 5

Horizontally Launched Projectiles.

A horizontally launched projectile moves at constant horizontal velocity while accelerating downward.

Imagine someone near a cliff edge kicking a pebble straight out, horizontally. Like every horizontally launched projectile, it starts with horizontal velocity and no vertical velocity. What happens as it falls?

Since horizontal motion doesn't affect vertical motion, it's easier to study each one separately. The left side of Figure 3 shows separate motion diagrams for the x- and y-components. In the horizontal diagram, every velocity vector is the same length, so the horizontal velocity isn't changing. The pebble isn't accelerating sideways. That's just what we'd expect, because after the kick, no horizontal force acts on it. In reality, air resistance would slow it a bit, but we're ignoring air resistance in this module.

In the vertical diagram, each velocity vector is a little longer than the one above it. So the vertical velocity is increasing, and the pebble is accelerating downward, at a sub y equals negative 9.8 meters per second squared. Again, that's expected, because gravity pulls downward. The vertical vectors change length because a force acts vertically; the horizontal vectors don't, because no force acts horizontally.

## Slide 6

The Parabolic Path.

Constant horizontal velocity plus uniform vertical acceleration makes a parabolic trajectory.

Treat the x- and y-motions separately, and each one is a straight line. But the right side of Figure 3 shows the real path, a parabola. At each moment, the horizontal and vertical components add together to make the total velocity vector, which is tangent to the parabola.

So the combination of a constant horizontal velocity and a steady vertical acceleration produces a trajectory with a parabolic shape.

## Slide 7

Problem-Solving Strategy, Motion in Two Dimensions.

Treat horizontal and vertical motion separately, linked by the same time.

Here's how to tackle projectile problems. First, draw a motion diagram with vectors at the starting and ending positions. If it's launched at an angle, also show the maximum height and the launch angle. Second, treat the vertical and horizontal motions separately, and list the known and unknown variables.

The motion equations: horizontally, at constant speed, final position equals v times t, plus initial position. Vertically, at constant acceleration, final velocity equals initial velocity plus a t. Final position equals initial position plus initial velocity times t, plus one half a t squared. And final velocity squared equals initial velocity squared plus 2 a times the change in position.

Third, for horizontal motion, the acceleration a sub x is 0.0 meters per second squared. For an angled launch, the vertical velocity at launch and when it falls back to the same height have the same size but opposite directions. Fourth, for vertical motion, a sub y is negative 9.8 meters per second squared, if up is positive, and for an angled launch, the vertical velocity at the highest point is zero. Fifth, pick the equations that find your unknowns, and apply them to horizontal and vertical motion separately. Time is the same for both, so solving for time in one direction gives you time for the other. Sixth, it can help to use just part of the path. You can choose any starting and ending points.

## Slide 8

Patterns in Projectile Motion.

Projectiles follow a repeating pattern of motion that can be found through evidence.

Here's a crosscutting challenge about patterns. Gather your own evidence to find the pattern of motion that projectiles follow.

Launch an object at a variety of angles and record the path it takes each time. Then create a presentation that shows what you found.

## Slide 9

Example Problem 1, A Sliding Plate.

Find the fall time from the vertical motion, then use it to find the horizontal distance.

You're making breakfast and slide a plate along the countertop. Oops, too fast! It flies off the end. If the countertop is 1.05 meters above the floor and the plate leaves it at 0.74 meters per second, how long does it take to fall, and how far from the counter does it land?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw horizontal and vertical motion diagrams. Put the origin at the top of the countertop, with positive x in the direction of the horizontal velocity and positive y up. Known: initial x and y are 0 meters, the initial horizontal velocity is 0.74 meters per second, the initial vertical velocity is 0 meters per second, a sub x is 0 meters per second squared, a sub y is negative 9.8 meters per second squared, and final y is negative 1.05 meters. Unknown: t and final x.

Step two: solve. Use the y-direction motion equation to find the time: final y equals initial y plus one half a sub y t squared. Rearranged, t equals the square root of 2 times the quantity final y minus initial y, over a sub y. That's the square root of 2 times negative 1.05 meters, over negative 9.8 meters per second squared, which is 0.46 seconds. Then use the x-direction equation: final x equals v sub x times t, which is 0.74 meters per second times 0.46 seconds, or 0.34 meters to the right of the counter.

Step three: evaluate. Time is in seconds and position is in meters. Both answers are positive, and the position sign matches the coordinate choice. And a fall of about a meter takes about half a second, so the plate should land about 0.5 seconds times 0.74 meters per second away, which matches.

## Slide 10

Angled Launches.

A projectile launched at an angle rises and falls symmetrically: its vertical speed at each height is the same going up and coming down.

When a projectile is launched at an angle, its initial velocity has both a vertical and a horizontal component. Launched upward, it's like a ball tossed straight up: it rises while slowing, stops for an instant at the top, and comes down speeding up.

The left diagram in Figure 4 shows the separate vertical and horizontal motion diagrams, with x horizontal and y vertical. Notice the symmetry. At every height, the object's vertical velocity on the way up has the same size as on the way down. Only the direction is opposite. Symmetry can help you find unknowns. For example, kick a ball off the ground with a vertical velocity of 1.2 meters per second up, and when it lands, its vertical velocity will be 1.2 meters per second down.

## Slide 11

Maximum Height, Range, and Flight Time.

The range is the horizontal distance a projectile travels when its initial and final heights are the same.

The right diagram in Figure 4 shows two important quantities. One is the maximum height, the projectile's height when its vertical velocity is zero and it has only its horizontal velocity. So the vertical velocity is zero right at the top of the path.

The other is the range, written R, the horizontal distance the projectile travels when it starts and ends at the same height. Not shown is the flight time, how long the projectile stays in the air. For football punts, flight time is often called hang time.

## Slide 12

Example Problem 2, The Flight of a Ball.

Use the vertical component of the launch velocity to find maximum height and flight time.

A ball is launched at 4.5 meters per second at 66 degrees above the horizontal. It starts and lands at the same height. What is its maximum height above its launch level, and what is its flight time?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Set up a coordinate system with the ball starting at the origin. Show the ball at the start, at its maximum height, and at the end, and show the direction of the net force. Draw a motion diagram showing v and a. Known: initial y is 0.0 meters, the launch angle is 66 degrees, the initial speed is 4.5 meters per second, the vertical velocity at the top is 0.0 meters per second, and a sub y is negative 9.8 meters per second squared. Unknown: the maximum height and t.

Step two: solve. Find the y-component of the initial velocity: 4.5 meters per second times the sine of 66 degrees, which is 4.1 meters per second. By symmetry, the final vertical velocity is negative 4.1 meters per second. For the maximum height, use vertical velocity at the top squared equals initial vertical velocity squared plus 2 a sub y times the height gained. At the top that velocity is zero, so the maximum height equals negative the initial vertical velocity squared, over 2 a sub y. That's negative the square of 4.1 meters per second, over 2 times negative 9.8 meters per second squared, or 0.86 meters.

For the time to return to launch height, use final vertical velocity equals initial vertical velocity plus a sub y t. So t equals the final minus the initial vertical velocity, over a sub y: negative 4.1 meters per second minus 4.1 meters per second, over negative 9.8 meters per second squared. That's 0.84 seconds.

Step three: evaluate. For something that rises less than 1 meter, a flight time under 1 second is reasonable.

## Slide 13

Forces from Air.

Forces from air, like wind and air resistance, can significantly change a projectile's motion.

So far we've ignored forces from the air. But think about why a kite stays up, or how a parachute lets a skydiver land safely. Forces from the air can change an object's motion a lot. For a basketball shot, that means gravity sets the arc, and air can nudge it too.

What about wind? Look at the three cases in Figure 6. In the top photo, water flows from a hose with almost no effect from the air. In the middle photo, wind blows in the same direction the water is moving. The air pushes the water forward, increasing its horizontal speed, so it travels farther. In the bottom photo, the wind changes direction. Now the air pushes against the water's motion, so it travels a shorter distance.

What if the wind is at an angle? Its horizontal component affects only horizontal motion, and its vertical component affects only vertical motion. A strong updraft, for example, could slow the water's downward speed. And even still air matters for some objects. Drop a sheet of paper held flat, and it drifts down slowly because of air resistance. The more surface area facing the moving air, the greater the air resistance.
